title: Critical points and monodromy: a geometric route to the symmetric group
subject: specialization
summary: In characteristic zero, simple critical points with distinct critical values determine the Galois group of a polynomial family. The branch permutations explain the generic group; specialization is a separate arithmetic step.
questionsAnswered: How can derivatives determine a generic Galois group?
Why do simple critical values produce transpositions?
Which parts of a generic result survive at a particular rational parameter?

sections.title: Critical points, critical values, and the generic polynomial
sections.body:
Let \(K\) have characteristic zero and let \(F\in K[X]\) have degree \(n\ge2\). The family \(F(X)-T\) is a polynomial over \(K(T)\), with \(T\) an indeterminate. A critical point is a root \(c\) of \(F'\), and its critical value is \(F(c)\). We call \(F\) Morse when \(F'\) has \(n-1\) distinct roots over \(\overline K\) and their critical values are pairwise distinct.

These are two separate tests. For \(F=X^4-2X^2\), the critical points \(0,1,-1\) are simple, but \(F(1)=F(-1)=-1\). A simple derivative alone does not satisfy the theorem. Composition \(F=(X^2)^2-2X^2\) also exposes an intermediate cover and a block system on the four generic roots.

The geometric group is the splitting-field group over \(\overline K(T)\); the arithmetic group is over \(K(T)\). Both act on the same \(n\) roots. A theorem about these groups does not assert the same group for every specialization \(T=t\).

sections.title: The Morse criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · Hilbert's Morse construction, characteristic-zero form

If \(F\in K[X]\) is Morse and \(\operatorname{char}K=0\), then

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Gal}(F(X)-T/\overline K(T))&=S_n,\\\operatorname{Gal}(F(X)-T/K(T))&=S_n.\end{aligned}\]

The splitting field over \(K(T)\) is regular over \(K\): it introduces no new algebraic constants.

The geometric conclusion is the decisive one. It gives a subgroup \(S_n\) of the arithmetic group, which already lies in \(S_n\). Equality follows, and the arithmetic/geometric quotient, which measures the constant extension, is trivial.

This is a sufficient criterion. Polynomials failing one of the Morse conditions can still have full symmetric monodromy; their ramification must be analyzed by another argument.

citations.note: The general theorem is applied after base change to the algebraic closure; arithmetic equality and regularity follow.

sections.title: Why the branch permutations generate enough transpositions
sections.body:
Proof sketch · ramification plus a connected graph

Over \(\overline K\), the degree-\(n\) cover \(X\mapsto F(X)\) is connected, so its monodromy group \(G\) is transitive. Equivalently, \(F(X)-T\) is irreducible over \(\overline K(T)\): in \(\overline K[X,T]\), a factor independent of \(T\) would have to divide the coefficient \(-1\) of \(T\).

At a simple critical point \(c\), the local expansion begins \(F(c)+a(X-c)^2+\cdots\), with \(a\ne0\). The distinct-value hypothesis ensures that only these two sheets meet over \(F(c)\). Its inertia generator is therefore a single transposition.

Let \(H\) be the normal subgroup generated by inertia at all finite branch values. The quotient of the Galois closure by \(H\) gives a connected degree-\(d\) cover of the projective line, unramified away from infinity. In characteristic zero all ramification is tame. If \(r\ge1\) points lie above infinity, Riemann–Hurwitz reads \(2g-2=-2d+(d-r)=-d-r\). Since \(g\ge0\), necessarily \(d=r=1\). Thus \(H=G\): the finite transpositions generate the whole group.

Make a graph whose vertices are the roots and whose edges are these transpositions, including their conjugates. Its connected components are the orbits of the generated group. Transitivity makes the graph connected, and edge transpositions of a connected graph generate every permutation. Hence \(G=S_n\).

The generation step matters. Merely finding one transposition inside a transitive group is insufficient.

citations.note: Inertia generation via Riemann–Hurwitz. The graph argument expands the transposition step.

sections.title: A family in every degree
sections.body:
Example · \(F(X)=X^n-X\)

For \(n\ge2\), the critical points satisfy \(nc^{n-1}=1\). They are nonzero and distinct, and

\[F(c)=-\frac{n-1}{n}c.\]

The critical values are therefore distinct. It follows that \(X^n-X-T\) has geometric and arithmetic group \(S_n\) in characteristic zero. Over \(\mathbb Q\), Hilbert irreducibility then supplies infinitely many rational parameters \(t\) for which \(X^n-X-t\) has group \(S_n\).

This construction separates two methods: derivatives and inertia determine the generic group, while Hilbert irreducibility supplies full-group fibers. To certify a specified \(t\), use factorization, discriminants, or resolvents for that fiber.

citations.note: The Morse theorem and specialization framework; the derivative calculation is supplied here.

sections.title: One cubic family, four different outcomes
sections.body:
For \(F=X^3-3X\), the critical points are \(\pm1\), with values \(\mp2\). Thus \(F(X)-T\) has generic group \(S_3\). Its discriminant is

\[\Delta(X^3-3X-T)=27(4-T^2).\]

Exact specializations over \(\mathbb Q\)

  • \(t=0\): \(X(X^2-3)\) is reducible; its splitting-field group is \(C_2\), fixing the rational root.
  • \(t=1\): \(X^3-3X-1\) has no rational root and discriminant \(81\), so its group is \(A_3=C_3\).
  • \(t=2\): \((X-2)(X+1)^2\) has a repeated root. This is a branch value, outside the separable-fiber setting.
  • \(t=3\): \(X^3-3X-3\) is Eisenstein at \(3\), and its discriminant is \(-135\), a nonsquare. Its group is \(S_3\).

Even away from the branch values, specialization can lower the group or destroy irreducibility. Conversely, a generic geometric argument can explain why many fibers have a large group without giving a certificate for any chosen one.

citations.note: Cubic discriminant formula and the irreducible cubic group test; specialized identities are checked directly.

sections.title: Characteristic and proof boundaries
sections.body:
The characteristic-zero hypothesis avoids wild ramification. In characteristic \(p\), the polynomial \(X^p-X\) has derivative \(-1\); its cover \(X^p-X=T\) is unramified at finite points, and its geometric group is the additive cyclic group of order \(p\), acting by \(X\mapsto X+a\) for \(a\in\mathbb F_p\). Ramification at infinity is wild. This shows why the tame step in the proof cannot simply be discarded.

There are positive-characteristic versions of the Morse theorem, but their hypotheses must be stated separately. The criterion above is intentionally restricted to characteristic zero.

related.why: Determine the generic group before asking which rational fibers retain it.
Inertia at a simple branch value supplies a transposition.
A transitive group generated by transpositions is symmetric.
Composition creates intermediate covers and block systems; collisions of critical values can reveal that structure.
The family X^n−X−T realizes every symmetric group regularly over Q(T).

questions.title: Does full symmetric generic monodromy force every separable rational fiber to have the same group?
questions.scope: The characteristic-zero Morse family X³−3X−T over Q
questions.body: No. At \(T=0\) the polynomial is reducible, and at \(T=1\) it is irreducible with group \(C_3\). Both fibers are separable. Hilbert irreducibility supplies many full-group fibers but does not remove all exceptions.
